subtitle: Journal-club style ICU update: PICO, key results, appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English.

script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for November 13, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 1 - National Early Warning Score 2-Guided Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle Car
sentences: Story 1 is about National Early Warning Score 2-Guided Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle Care for Adults With Suspected Sepsis in the Emergency Department: A Hybrid Type 1 Effectiveness-Implementation Stepped-Wedge Randomized Controlled Trial Pilot Study (NEWS-1 TRIPS)..
This is a randomized / clinical trial from Critical care medicine.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in Critically ill or ICU-relevant patients described in the abstract; confirm eligibility criteria in the full text., how should we interpret Exposure or intervention stated in the title/objective. compared with Comparator or control group stated in the methods/results, if present.?
All progression criteria were met, except for suboptimal overall bundle compliance (56.1%).

Exploratory intention-to-treat analysis (standard care group, n = 102; NEWS-1 group, n = 98) showed no significant between-group difference in 30-day all-cause mortality (standard care group, 3.9%; NEWS-1 group, 9.2%; absolute risk difference, 5.3%; 95% CI -1.6% to 12.1%); in-hospital, 90-day all-cause, or sepsis-related mortality; need for mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, intensive care, or surgery; or ventilator-free days and adverse events.
The primary outcome was the feasibility of a full-scale hybrid trial, evaluated based on 14 progression criteria.
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.
The bedside implication is this: This may refine antibiotic selection in selected infected patients, but it should be integrated with local microbiology, renal risk, stewardship, and source control.
Useful English phrase: these findings should be interpreted cautiously because the details of design and applicability matter.

script.heading: Story 2 - Global Prevalence of Obstetric Causes of Critical Illness in P
sentences: Story 2 is about Global Prevalence of Obstetric Causes of Critical Illness in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis..
This is a systematic review / meta-analysis from Critical care medicine.

script.heading: Story 3 - Composite Endpoints in Critical Care Delirium Trials.
sentences: Story 3 is about Composite Endpoints in Critical Care Delirium Trials..
This is a recent research article from Critical care medicine.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in critically ill patients, in which a person's attention and awareness change acutely, how should we interpret Exposure or intervention stated in the title/objective. compared with Comparator or control group stated in the methods/results, if present.?

articles.title: National Early Warning Score 2-Guided Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle Care for Adults With Suspected Sepsis in the Emergency Department: A Hybrid Type 1 Effectiveness-Implementation Stepped-Wedge Randomized Controlled Trial Pilot Study (NEWS-1 TRIPS).
articles.summary: Adult patients of 18 years or older with a clinical diagnosis of infection requiring hospitalization and a NEWS-2 greater than or equal to 5. Implementation of the Hour-1 Bundle when NEWS-2 was greater than or equal to 5. All progression criteria were met, except for suboptimal overall bundle compliance (56.1%). Exploratory intention-to-treat analysis (standard care group, n = 102; NEWS-1 group, n = 98) showed no significant between-group difference in 30-day all-cause mortality (standard care group, 3.9%; NEWS-1 group, 9.2%; absolute risk difference, 5.3%; 95% CI -1.6% to 12.1%); in-hospital, 90-day all-cause, or sepsis-related mortality; need for mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, intensive care, or surgery; or ventilator-free days and adverse events. To increase the uptake of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle, we implemented a novel sepsis care model (National Early Warning Score [NEWS]-1 care), in which the Hour-1 Bundle is objectively triggered by a high NEWS-2 (≥ 5).

articles.title: Global Prevalence of Obstetric Causes of Critical Illness in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.summary: The pooled prevalence was estimated using a random-effects model with 95% CIs. Of the 3,735 total records, 50 studies met the eligibility criteria, encompassing 7,756,232 women receiving obstetric care in tertiary hospitals across 20 countries, with 49,299 ICU admissions. Globally, 1.0% (95% CI, 0.8-1.3%) of pregnant and postpartum women experience critical illness and require admission to an ICU. The frequency varies according to the country's income levels, with the highest in low-income countries (4.1%) and the lowest in high-income countries (0.5%). Notably, 72.3% of ICU admissions were attributed to known obstetric causes, primarily obstetric hemorrhage (23.3%) and hypertension in pregnancy (26.9%).

articles.title: Composite Endpoints in Critical Care Delirium Trials.
articles.summary: Given these challenges, delirium trials have adopted one of two composite endpoints: delirium- and coma-free days, defined as the number of days alive without delirium or coma for both survivors and nonsurvivors, and an alternative composite that ranks death as the worst state and orders days alive without delirium or coma among survivors. Delirium is an abnormal mental status, commonly occurring among critically ill patients, in which a person's attention and awareness change acutely. Delirium is associated with negative outcomes, including death. Furthermore, a longer duration of delirium is associated with long-term cognitive impairment in survivors of critical illness. Hence, there is a need for novel interventions that reduce the duration of delirium; however, measuring and analyzing "duration of delirium" as an endpoint in randomized trials is challenging due to the episodic nature of delirium and the competing events of coma and death, which can bias analyses of duration of delirium.
